annotations.text: THE P-J PRESS BUREAU, 908 Walnut Street, Philadelphia.

The survivors of Cavalry Post No. 35, G.A.R., the only cavity post of the Grand Army in Philadelphia, have set up a unique exhibit at post headquarters. It is the figure of a horse made up entirely of army and equippments used by the veterans during the Civil War. Carbines form the spreading legs of the curious device, stirrup leathers and cartridge boxes make the hoops, a soldier plume the tail, an army revolver the curve of the hip, a similar weapon, butt down, the curve of the nostrils. The back is outlined in sabres, and bugles, swords and revolvers are spread around where needed to help out the queer formation.

CHILDREN SEEK COOL AND SHADE OF PARKS, FLEEING
OPPRESSIVE HEAT AND PARALYSIS PLAGUE.
Little children standing in line at a park fountain patiently waiting their turn to get a drink.

The parks and other spots of green throughout the city are crowded with children of all ages seeking relief from the oppressive heat and fusing the danger of infantile paralysis that lurks in narrow dirty streets and ill-kept tenements.

More heat and more humidity is the gloomy message issued to the sweltering cities. The great heat is the plague's ally. Not until the autumn brings cooler weather is there much hope of a decline in the epidemic.

KILLING OF ARMED NEUTRALITY BILL REMOVES HOPE OF RELIEF OF FREIGHT CONGESTION.

The consequences of the killing of the Armed Neutral Bill are far-reaching. New York and many of the other seaport cities suffer thereby from a great commercial evil - freight congestion. Ship owners demand that their vessels be armed or conveyed and this failing they will tie up their vessels until suitable relief is arranged for.

Mountains of freight of all sorts and descriptors bank the streets, docks and piers along the east and west waterfronts of New York City. The barges have been transferred from trains and fighters and stacked on the docks waiting marine shipment abroad.

Millions upon millions of dollars are represented in this enormous amount of bulk and instead of being gradually shipped overseas it is increasing to tremendous proportions day by day.

Great hopes had been placed in the passage of his Armed Neutrality Bill and when this measure failed to pass all hope of immediate relief was removed.

USE OF WHALE AS WAR FOOD SHOWN AT LUN CHEON.

From left to right are Arthur Williams, New York Food Administrator, President Henry P. Osborn and Admiral Robert E. Peary at the whale lunch at the American Museum of Natural History. Except for the ice cream, coffee and vegetables every dish on the menu was composed either entirely or in part of whale. There was whale steak and many other forms of whale. The purpose of the lunchson was to show the suitability of whale meat as a food especially now because of the war time stringency of beef and pork. 2/8/18.

George B. Lennox is now a travelling man - after trying many ventures in up-State towns and cities, Mr. Lennox has finally struck the job he claims is his - travelling. For more than a month, Mr. Lennox and his family have been living in his unique hotel on the Leister state, on the upper end of Manhattan, Mr. Lennox, a handy man with carpenters tools has made his own hotel, for his wife and daughter and with this novel residence will sooner or later beging his drive to the coast. In this way he plans to greatly reduce his cost of living and at the same time get all the enjoyment possible out of life. Photo shows Mrs. Lennox using the bottom of the trailer for an ice-box. 5/31/22.

TROOPERS OF 11th CAVALRY, RELEASED BY MEXICANS, ARRIVE IN ET PASO, TEXAS.

Trocers of the 11th Cavalry, released by Mexicans after capture at Carrizal and detention in prison, grouped smiling and happy on the U.S. end of the International Bridge, which connects El Paso, Texas, with Juarez, Mexico. Knelling in the centre of the first row with white hat on his head is Jim Spillsbury, U.S. scout and interpreter attached to the 11th Cavalry who was also held captive with troopers by Carranza forces.
Upon their arrival on American soil each cavityman was presented with a bouquet, and then given a kerosene bath and a pair of blue overalls and a jacket to match.

FAIR "ROOKIES" BREAKING IN AT THE CHEVY CHASE CAMP.
Students at the Chevy Chase camp going through setting exercises.

The National Service camp is now in full swing. Drills are given by an officer of the army and are purely gymnastic, no firearms being in the camp. The work of keeping, not only the tents but the company streets, in order is done entirely by the women pupils. It is not an unfamiliar sight to see several prominent debautantes of last Winter picking paper from the grass about the officers' tents. All must pitch in and do their share. Many prominent Washington women are at the camp taking the course of instruction. When Mrs. Barnett, wife of Ilaj. Gen. Barnett of the Marine Corps enters the camp to stay she will be joined by Mrs. Clarke and Ilaj. James H. Thompson, wife and daughter of the Speaker. Mrs. Robert Lansing, wife of Secretary of State Lansing, has joined the school and is wearing the regulation $10.50 uniform. Mrs. Lansing is proud to be a "rockie" and is much interested in the work of the camp. 5/4/16.

COMMANDANT AND STAFF OF THE NATIONAL SERVICE SCHOOL
AT CHEVY CHASE, WASHINGTON, D.C.
Commandant Miss Elizabeth E. Poe and her Staff of the National Service School at Chevy Chase, Wash. D.C.

From left to right: Mrs. B.R.Russel, Wash., D.C. Aldc, Miss Vella Poe Wilson, Wash., D.C. Adjt. Miss Natalie Lincoln, Wash., D.C., Major. Miss Elizabeth E. Poe, Wash., D.C., Commandant. Miss Mary Baker, Wildwood, N.J., Aide, Miss Anne Tracy, New York, Major. Mrs. H.B. Joy, Detroit, Mich., Aide, Chief of Staff.

The camp is in the hands of this group of capable directors, who all wear the regulation khaki uniform. These are busy days for the Staff, with so many fair young ladies to take care of. Everything at the camp is running smoothly, drills go on, meals are served regularly, and no illness or injuries have been reported excepting many cases of blistered feet; as a consequence "sneakers" appear on drill under the very natty skirts that with Norfolk jackets and soft felt hats comprise a most attractive uniform. 5/4/16.

SIXTEEN YEAR OLD GIRL $A$K$S WORLD
RECORD ON RIFLE RANGE.

Elizabeth Dean a sixteen-year old high school girl in Cambridge, Mass., by shooting 31 consecutive bullsets on a 300 yard riff range with a regulation army Springfield rifle has set a world's record for a girl. The slip of a girl went on to the Massachusetts rifle range at Wakefield, Mass with her uncle's Lisut.Harry J.Dugans of Co.A., 8th Mass.Regiment,M.V.M. and without a shoulder pad, thrice fired the ten shots allowed her fist for each round and scored perfect bull's eyes. The thirty-first shot was a hit, but on the next she just touched the ring nearest the center of the target and thus stopped. She was surrounded by an admiring crowd of soldiers and marines who watched her work with abated breath. The girl loves out of deer life and expects to enter the famous school conducted in Cambridge by Dr.Sargent for girls, where gymnastics and out-of-door sports form a part of the program of the schools educational features. WOMEN APPROPRIATELY DRESSED TAKE UP NEW'S WORK PREPARING FOR EVENTUALITIES.
Left to right: Miss Jean Dean Barnes, Mrs. E.H. Woodward, Mrs. A. C. Park, and Mrs. I. L. Hill, dressed in bloomers learning the ins and outs of ambulance driving, N.Y.C. at Y.

The "Preparedness" cry has been taken up by the women of the country and rings through the States. From the Atlantic to the Pacific, from the Gulf to the Canadian Border women are looking about them determining just what branch of public service they are best fitted for.

Should trouble arise with a foreign power and cut men called to the ranks in great numbers we may see out tellleys, busses, private cars, and even delivery trucks chauff-ferred by women. Fair ladies will serve as mechanics and fulfill duties as elevator runners, "trainmen", "milkmen", and perhaps if the need arises may be placed on the various police forces. The possibilities for service are almost unnumbered. It has been proven to abroad that women are competent workers in nearly all lines now operated by men and in many factories and plants in England and Canada women are the male, men the exception.

MACHINE GUN CAN BE MOUNTED ON ORDINARY AUTO FOR DEFENSE PURPOSES.

If you own an automobile, you have a likely defense weapon in your possession. The photo shows Mr. and Mrs. H. M. Busch in their automobile showing how the machine gun can be mounted on the car to be used for defense purposes.

It is proposed as a Home Defense Measure to, station machine guns at points throughout cities and suburban stations, so that in case of no-essity, the people with automobile cars can rush to these points, minimize the maximum pressure, get the guns, mount them on their machines, and be ready for action. The machine gun can be used as an anti-aircraft gun, and would be an effective defense against air raddles, if such ever occur. Mr. and Mrs. Busch are pouring to show the people the value of the idea and to demonstrate how the gun is mounted.

Every automobile that will hot be used for other military purposes can be converted into a fighting machine. It doesn't make any differences how small the machine is, it can serve the purpose just as well.

DESIGNER OF NEW TYPE OF BATTLEPLANE AND WIFE
WHO COMMANDS MACHINE GUT AND TORPEDO BOMBS.

Newly modeled battleplans which carries Lewis machining gun and torpedo bombs, ready for flight over the aviation grounds at Hempstead, L.I. Mr. A. S. Heinrich, who sits at the pilot's wheel, is the designer of this, the first battleplane of its kind exhibited in this country. The machine is equipped with a device for carrying five torpedo bombs. They are attached underneath the body of the car and can be released by observer. Mounted on the bow of the car is a Lewis machine gun, otherwise known as the "Belgian Rattlesnake". Mr. Heinrich hopes that the U.S. Government will adopt this battleplans for its aeronautic fleet. 9/14/16.

MILLIONS OF SHOES AND PUTTERS BEING RUSHED FOR
UNCLE SAM'S FIGHTERS.
Upper photo shows Government inspectors looking over the different parts of the shoes before the assembling. All government work receives a careful scrutiny from the inspectors before it is accepted.
Lower photo films: Many women are employed in the different plants where shoes and putters are manufactured for the Government. They are shown in the photo putting laces in the canvas putters.

Millions of shoes and puttees are being manufactured for Uncle San's fighters. There is no great length of time for the footwear to be manufactured in, and the work has to be rushed with the utmost speed, for the time when the second. National Army contingent will be called in approaching and all the equipment must be ready. These scenes are typical of the many great plants working without a stop to run out the immense quantities required.

Healthy Fisher Folk.
Wonderful Strength and Endurance due to Fish Diet.

Have you ever noticed how healthy and happy all the fisherfolk look one meets at the seaside? Sea air, you say. Yes, certainly, sea air; but also the silver treasures they draw up, often at the risk of their lives, from the blue depths of the sea—Fish

That is the food they eat; that is their staple diet; day in, day out, the year round. And the men are the men who man our lifeboats, the men we want in our Dreadnoughts and merchant service, the men whom Shackleton and Peary take with them into the fastnesses of the ice-bound North and South.
It is the same with the wives and daughters. All of them are living pictures of health.

The explanation is not far to seek. As Sir James Crichton Browne, M.D., has pointed out, the food value of fish is enormous. It is easily digested, and when it is digested nearly the whole of it is absorbed into the system. That is where the strength and endurance come from.
Among town dwellers fish is eaten perhaps one day in the week, and meat the other six. "Were the proportion the other way the benefit to health and pocket alike would soon be apparent.

Perhaps it is the monotony usually found in fish-cooking that accounts for the general neglect of this most wholesome and nutritious diet. If so, that difficulty is now overcome by the publication of a clever little cookery book which treats entirely of the various ways in which fish may be cooked.

And the number of these ways is truly surprising. There are clearly explained recipes for soups, pies, puddings, cakes, and endless other delightful dishes, all made from fish, given in this wonderful little work—which is entitled, "Tasty Ways of Cooking Fish"—as well as explicit directions for frying fish as it should be fried, and boiling it as it should be boiled.
